entries.title: Supporting AI readiness in higher education
entries.summary: Graduation caps and icons in different colors
entries.content:
Editor’s note: This week we’re joining thousands of faculty and administrators at EDUCAUSE, one of the United States’ biggest higher education technology exhibitions. Visit us at Booth #700, where you can see demos of Gemini for Education, Gemini Notebook, and the latest Google Cloud AI solutions. Follow along on X and Facebook for the latest updates.

As higher education leaders gather this week at the EDUCAUSE Annual Conference, AI is undoubtedly top of mind for all. While this technology offers significant opportunities to support students, faculty, and staff, many institutions — especially community colleges and public university systems — face resource constraints. Recent studies indicate that 41% of higher-ed educators say they have not received any formal training on using AI tools in learning environments.

To help close this gap, Google.org is supporting two higher education initiatives focused on keeping educators at the heart of using AI:

Supporting adult learners

Despite making up at least a third of higher education enrollments for decades, adult learners 25 and older are more likely to drop out, returning for their second year at a rate 35 percentage points lower than traditional-age students.

To address systemic barriers for these students, the Coalition of Urban Serving Universities (USU), in partnership with the Association of Public and Land-grant Universities (APLU), is enhancing its Urban Adult Learner Institute (UALI).

Supported by Google.org, USU is integrating Grow with Google resources and AI-integrated lessons into its professional development certification. By equipping higher education practitioners, including faculty and advisors, with practical, hands-on tasks, schools can offer students better career guidance and help them succeed. Educators across 30 universities will test these new methods so other schools can easily replicate what works to ensure success for adult learners.

Creating new models for career-connected learning

While traditional internships have long been the standard for career readiness, overwhelming demand from students and employers has created a need for scalable new approaches.

To meet this moment, USU is leading a project to scale career-focused community-based learning (CBL) enhanced by AI. Over the next 15 months, USU will collect and qualitatively analyze 10 models at member institutions, publish case studies, and convene a working group to develop a research and practice agenda. The initiative will create flexible work-based learning pathways across diverse academic disciplines, expanding workforce readiness for a wide range of students.

Reimagining strategic planning

Strategic planning at community colleges is often treated as a compliance exercise rather than an engine for innovation. Through its Reimagining Community Colleges (RCC) initiative, Education Design Lab (The Lab) is helping two-year institutions transform that dynamic and prepare students for the future of work with support from Google.org.

Following a successful summit of educators this week and a cohort of five colleges launching redesign plans, a new national competition will launch in early 2027 for a state-level community college system to undergo a two-year initiative to use technology-enabled solutions to better serve their students. This upcoming phase will apply The Lab’s Future of Learning framework to build scalable, durable solutions that strengthen continuous innovation across campuses.

To explore free training resources and learn more about our education initiatives, visit the Google for Education Learning Center or connect with our teams this week at EDUCAUSE.

entries.title: Let skills in Gemini tackle your most repetitive tasks
entries.content:
With skills, you can save your most-used instructions once and run them endlessly — so you can skip the repetitive prompting and jump straight to the results. Skills are already available in Gemini Spark, and they will soon replace Gems as the tool for tailoring instructions for specific tasks.

Today, we’re rolling out skills directly into Gemini chat globally 1 , and bringing this functionality to Google Workspace business, enterprise, nonprofit, and education customers in the coming weeks.

Save time with reusable instructions

Once you create a skill, you can easily use it again just by typing a forward slash ‘/’ and the skill’s name directly in the prompt bar.

Here are a few ways skills can help you work more efficiently:

  • Prepare for presentations: Build a custom skill to outline slides, craft talking points, and prep for tough Q&As, whether for a class presentation or a project pitch.
  • Match your writing style: Gemini knows your unique writing style across Workspace apps to speed up drafting, all while keeping you in full control.
  • Get more perspectives: Ask Gemini to always provide three to five distinct viewpoints on a topic to help you brainstorm ideas, refine arguments, or commit to a decision.

Gemini can help you build custom skills from your chats and automatically run them whenever you enter a matching prompt. For bigger tasks, you can stack multiple skills together at the same time — like combining a writing style skill with a brand guidelines skill to create on-brand assets in your voice. Plus, starting today, you can create skills that include reference files like plain text documents, PDFs, or images.

Transition from Gems

In the coming weeks, skills will have the features you loved in Gems, including the ability to share them with others and add files from Google Drive and notebooks from Gemini Notebook. As we bring more functionality to skills, we will remove support for Gems starting in November for individuals with personal accounts, March 2027 for Workspace business, enterprise, and nonprofit customers, and June 2027 for Workspace education customers. As part of this change, Opal 2 , our experiment for building mini apps will also turn down at the same time in November (learn more).

To make this transition seamless, we will automatically migrate your Gems into skills when Gems go away. You can learn more about how to transition your Gems into skills by visiting our help center.

entries.title: Celebrating International Translation Day: Meet 3 linguistic experts behind Google Translate
entries.summary: The illustration shows people around the world using Google Translate.
entries.content:
For more than 20 years, Google Translate has helped people break down language barriers. Now, by pairing our latest Gemini models with human perspective, we’re turning literal translations into natural conversations. This International Translation Day, meet three Googlers on the Translate team who are bridging the gap between cutting-edge technology and human connection.

Janneke Van Hofwegen, User Experience Research Manager

Janneke’s passion for language dates back to 2002, when she started teaching at an international university in Lithuania. While learning Lithuanian, she began to view language as a reflection of identity and belonging.

Over the next two decades in linguistics, she explored how language shapes self-expression and behavior across lifetimes. She earned a Ph.D. from Stanford and co-authored “African American Language: Language Development from Infancy to Adulthood,” which won the Linguistic Society of America's Leonard Bloomfield Book Award.

Today, she brings her expertise to Google Translate, where she leads the team that tests early features with everyday users to ensure translations reflect real, human conversation rather than literal phrasing. Her academic research, which showed that language is constantly evolving, is now being applied alongside our latest Gemini models to ensure Google translations capture the living, dynamic nuance of conversation and not just the literal words.

Isaac Caswell, Software Engineer

Isaac’s interest in linguistics began in the Gaeltacht, the region of Ireland where the Irish language is still spoken as a native language. Spending time with his Irish-speaking family there showed him the importance of preserving languages, particularly in an increasingly globalized world. In 2017, he joined Google Translate, where he focused on expanding support for digitally under-represented languages, helping add 146 new languages to the platform. (Today, there are almost 250 languages on Translate.)

Isaac has worked with communities around the world to preserve native languages. He’s built transliteration tools — which map words from an alphabet so you can read and pronounce them — alongside Canadian Inuktut groups and Santali activists, and helped everyone from Maldivian academics to frontline healthcare workers in Timor-Leste and The Gambia.

While AI supercharges modern-day translations, Isaac says the human experience of actually speaking a different language is something technology can’t replace. Today, he focuses on supporting languages with limited available digital data. By combining community involvement with computational linguistics, he’s ensuring speakers of data-scarce languages aren’t left behind.

Harsh Shah, Software Engineer

Since joining Google in 2018, Harsh has shaped foundational language tools, including interactive, accent-tailored pronunciation guides and Search’s large-scale grammar checker. For nearly five years, he’s led the Search translation experience with a focus on solving for linguistic context so users get accurate meanings instead of literal definitions.

As technology advances rapidly, Harsh is dedicated to humanizing translations by prompting users for context just as an interpreter would. Working alongside human experts, he fine-tunes large language models to accurately judge nuance. By pairing linguistic precision with AI, he helps Translate bring smarter, culturally grounded learning tools to more languages, faster.

Technology can translate words, but it takes real people to translate meaning. By pairing our latest AI models with the experiences of linguistic experts, we’re ensuring anyone, anywhere, can be understood with Google Translate.

entries.title: Waze rolls out new features to support Breast Cancer Awareness Month.
entries.summary: This October, Waze will help drivers find screening clinics, assess their health risks, and schedule routine checkups.
entries.content:
This October, Waze is introducing new features for Breast Cancer Awareness Month to help drivers find screening clinics, assess their health risks, and schedule routine checkups. Drivers everywhere can show support on the road by switching their vehicle icon to a custom pink car.

In the U.S., Waze has partnered with National Breast Cancer Foundation so drivers can find thousands of screening centers right on the map, and easily navigate to them. In Israel, through a partnership with One in Nine, Waze will show drivers nearby breast health clinics and send an email with quick access to risk assessment questionnaires. Drivers in Israel can also turn on voice guidance from comedian Adi Ashkenazi, who will share reminders to schedule routine screenings.

These features are live now and will be available throughout October. To access them, download the latest version of Waze on Android or iOS.

entries.title: We’re introducing SynthID Bio, bringing our watermarking technology to synthetic biology.
entries.summary: Google DeepMind introduces SynthID Bio to watermark AI-designed proteins while maintaining biological function. Read the full research report here.
entries.content:
Today, we’re introducing SynthID Bio, a new technology that watermarks AI-designed proteins while preserving their biological function.

SynthID Bio embeds an imperceptible, verifiable watermark directly into biological designs, such as AI-generated protein sequences and predicted 3D structures.

In laboratory tests across target proteins, our watermarked designs successfully matched the performance and natural diversity of unwatermarked versions. This creates a vital provenance layer to strengthen biosecurity and preserve the integrity of open scientific databases.

You can read the full blog post and research on the Google DeepMind website.

entries.title: Game on: Henry Cavill is putting Googlebook to the test
entries.summary: : Actor Henry Cavill, with a mustache, wearing a brown ribbed knit sweater and jeans, sits at a large rustic wooden table resting his hand on an open Googlebook.
entries.content:
Laptops need to keep up with our growing creative and professional ambitions. Crafted for performance and designed for Gemini Intelligence, Googlebook does exactly that. It brings you powerful hardware with unique software experiences like Continue on phone syncing, Rambler speech-to-text, Antigravity and so much more. To help showcase the potential of this next-generation laptop, we found a partner who understands the power of great technology to unlock creativity and bring ideas to life. Actor, producer, and tech enthusiast Henry Cavill is putting Googlebook to the test.

We recently met with Henry to discuss his own creative ambitions and the conversation quickly turned to the need for a laptop that could keep up with him and work seamlessly with his Android phone. Henry doesn't just play complex characters on screen; he manages multiple ventures behind the scenes — including his own production company — all while maintaining a passion for gaming, fantasy lore, and high-performance technology. Now, he is using Googlebook to build his personal passion projects.

To kick off our partnership, we couldn’t resist the chance to tap Henry's inner maker. This November, Henry is teaming up with Google to build a video game using Googlebook. Stay tuned to see what he’s creating, and discover how Googlebook is redefining what a laptop can do.

entries.title: Experience two artists’ perspectives on philosophy, science, and AI
entries.summary: A behind the scenes video introducing the residency collaboration
entries.content:
How can artists use technology to deepen our understanding of life, matter, and consciousness? That’s the question two artists sought to answer during the Online Artist Residency with LAS Art Foundation in collaboration with Google Arts & Culture.

The residency set out to support artists in exploring digital world building and the simulation of living systems, with the two artists selected for their exceptional technical skill and artistic imagination.

Artists Xin Liu and Eunjo Lee used Google AI tools to create “nom nom” (Xin Liu) and “In Your Eyes, Before My Own” (Eunjo Lee) — two artworks exploring frontier AI research.

“nom nom” by Xin Liu

In “nom nom,” Xin explores how collective intelligence naturally arises when millions of small particles interact. To craft the project, she drew on research into artificial life and emergent computation by Googler researchers Blaise Agüera y Arcas and Alexander Mordvintsev, and the concept of Neural Cellular Automata (NCAs) — models where millions of particles form, compete, and dissolve into a living ecology. See for yourself in this video that guides you through the experience.

“I want to explore an image of intelligence distributed across millions of tiny neural networks that react only to their surroundings — not as a singular mind above the world, but as a living ecology of fragments,” Xin says.

Xin Liu, nom nom (2026). Commissioned by LAS Art Foundation in collaboration with Google Arts & Culture.

“In Your Eyes, Before My Own” by Eunjo Lee

Eunjo’s “techno-alchemy” process bridges ancient philosophy, linguistics, and modern psychology. She sees technology as a medium that reveals the philosophical and psychological underpinnings of our physical and digital existence.

For this project, Eunjo converted hand-drawn sketches into 3D assets using Nano Banana and Veo. She then layered motion-captured choreography onto characters and mapped Korean Hangul phonetics over the 3D environment to create a linguistic system that reflected the landscape’s geometry.

“This commission opened up a vast alchemical laboratory,” Eunjo says. “As the [Buddhist] philosophy of Indra's net posits that all entities reflect one another to form a colossal web, this concept manifests today through the neural network.”

Eunjo Lee, In Your Eyes, Before My Own (2026). Commissioned by LAS Art Foundation in collaboration with Google Arts & Culture.

Experience “nom nom” and “In Your Eyes, Before My Own” on Google Arts & Culture and las-art.foundation today.

entries.title: Google is a technology partner for the launch of America.gov.
entries.summary: Google partners with America.gov to use Gemini to help 100 million people access federal services faster. See how we are modernizing public access.
entries.content:
Today, the White House announced America.gov, a streamlined "front door" designed to simplify how citizens access federal services online. Google is proud to be named a technology partner in this vital initiative, leveraging Gemini to help more than 100 million people access critical public resources with greater speed and ease.

By supporting the administration’s vision for digital modernization, we are committed to making these everyday public services seamless, accessible, and responsive for all Americans.

entries.title: Watch the winning trailer from the Future Vision XPRIZE, The Gifted.
entries.summary: Watch the winning trailer from the Future Vision XPRIZE, The Gifted.
entries.content:
Earlier this year, we partnered with XPRIZE and Range Media Partners to launch the Future Vision XPRIZE, a global competition calling for films that envision a hopeful, technology-enabled future. Last week in Los Angeles, independent filmmaker Jeff Synthesized was named the grand prize winner for The Gifted.

Inspired by a deeply personal story, the film centers on an 11-year-old boy who recreates his late mother’s voice and essence out of love and code. What emerges across the town’s networks quietly cares for his entire community — reflecting the filmmaker’s belief that technology’s greatest promise lies in empathy and human connection.

Chosen from more than 2,500 entries worldwide, the solo-developed project receives $100,000 alongside $2.5 million in feature production funding. Through Google’s 100 ZEROS initiative, we are partnering with Range Media Partners to help bring this story to the big screen.

entries.title: Google Arts & Culture turns 15 — and gives its app a makeover
entries.summary: Celebrating 15 years of Google Arts & Culture with a new app experience YouTube video
entries.content:
Over the past 15 years, Google Arts & Culture has partnered with more than 3,000 cultural institutions and artists across more than 90 countries. Working alongside this vibrant ecosystem, our goal has always been to preserve and make the world’s art and culture accessible to everyone, while creating experiences that educate, inspire, and delight.

Starting today, you can check out our refreshed Google Arts & Culture mobile app to mark this 15-year milestone. The updated experience helps you easily navigate our partners’ vast archives, including high-resolution artworks, archaeological 3D artifacts, fashion, performance art, sports, craft, culinary heritage, natural history, science, design, and nature.

A new way to ask and see

At the heart of this update is a new conversational search: ask any question about arts and culture, and get an answer that pairs insightful explanations with visuals and curated stories from partner archives.

Ask anything that sparks your curiosity — whether you're delving into ‘Caravaggio’s chiaroscuro,’ finding ‘impressionist museums in Paris,’ browsing ‘images captured by the Webb telescope,’ wondering ‘what are bento boxes,’ or simply taking a moment to admire ‘cats in art.’

Ask questions in your own words, and get visual, grounded answers.

An all-new homepage

The redesigned homepage brings together the entire app into a single feed built for quick daily discovery. Modular sections surface bite-sized cultural stories, daily highlights, and direct access to interactive features. This includes two new AI experiments: Chrono Look, which lets you virtually try on historical attire across different eras through sketches and realistic renderings, and Dial-an-Artist, an interactive tool for simulated conversations with historical figures about their work. Plus, check out an expanded City Guide, featuring 27 newly added destinations with local cultural landmarks and real-time cultural events.

The updated Google Arts & Culture app is rolling out globally starting today. Download or update now on Google Play and the Apple App Store to explore the next chapter of cultural discovery.
